name: Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes Including Aplastic Anemia and Myelodysplasia

clinicalPearls: Marrow failure cytopenias reflect deficient production, distinguishing them from peripheral destruction (hemolysis, ITP, immune leukopenia, hypersplenism); the syndromes are categorized by the dominant marrow morphology, with aplastic anemia (fatty/empty marrow), MDS (dysplastic marrow), and single-lineage aplasias forming a related spectrum.

Immune (acquired) aplastic anemia is classically a young person's disease with abrupt pancytopenia in a previously well adolescent or young adult; the age distribution is biphasic with peaks in the teens-twenties and again in older adults.

In aplastic anemia bleeding (bruising, gum oozing, epistaxis, menorrhagia, petechiae) is typically the earliest symptom, whereas infection as a first symptom is unusual; lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly are highly atypical and should prompt search for another cause of pancytopenia.

Clues to an inherited bone marrow failure syndrome: short stature and cafe au lait spots with thumb/radial anomalies (Fanconi anemia); dystrophic nails, mucosal leukoplakia and reticular hyperpigmentation (dyskeratosis congenita); premature hair graying plus a family history of pulmonary or hepatic fibrosis (telomere biology disorders); recurrent warts and unusual infections (GATA2 deficiency).

A detectable PNH clone by flow cytometry is found in up to half of patients at presentation of aplastic anemia and strongly suggests immune-mediated pathophysiology and likely responsiveness to immunosuppression; patients can later cross over between aplastic and hemolytic PNH phenotypes.

MDS is predominantly a disease of older adults (mean onset over 70) with a slight male predominance; anemia (often macrocytic) dominates the early course and at least half of patients are asymptomatic, discovered incidentally on routine blood counts.

Persistent parvovirus B19 infection is a treatable cause of pure red cell aplasia; the marrow shows giant pronormoblasts (the cytopathic signature), and diagnosis requires detection of viral DNA because IgG/IgM antibodies are commonly absent in immunodeficient hosts.

B19 parvovirus uses the erythrocyte P antigen as its receptor; in patients with underlying hemolysis it can precipitate a transient aplastic crisis with abrupt worsening of anemia from arrested erythropoiesis.

Macrocytosis (elevated MCV) is a frequent finding across marrow failure states; in aplastic anemia the smear shows large red cells with a paucity of platelets and granulocytes, near-absent reticulocytes, and the elevated MCV often persists even after recovery.

Marrow blast percentage is the strongest morphologic prognostic determinant in MDS; the WHO threshold of 20% marrow blasts separates AML from MDS, and blasts should be enumerated manually on smear and by flow cytometry.

5q deletion MDS arises from heterozygous loss of a ribosomal protein gene, effectively mimicking constitutional red cell aplasia; SF3B1 mutation is strongly associated with ring sideroblasts and a relatively favorable outcome.

Severity grading in aplastic anemia and recovery thresholds are defined by blood counts (see severity criteria); absolute reticulocyte and lymphocyte numbers are better predictors of treatment response than the classic severity definition in the immunosuppression era.
harrison.pathophysiology: Bone marrow failure results from severe damage to the hematopoietic cell compartment. In aplastic anemia the marrow is replaced by fat, CD34+ early hematopoietic cells are greatly diminished, and the stem cell pool in severe disease may be reduced to about 1% or less of normal. Three principal mechanisms underlie an empty marrow: physical/chemical damage (high-dose radiation, benzene and its reactive hydroquinone/quinolone metabolites, cytotoxic chemotherapy), immune-mediated stem cell destruction, and constitutional genetic defects. Acquired aplastic anemia is most often immune: activated cytotoxic T cells suppress hematopoietic progenitors, type 1 cytokines including interferon-gamma upregulate Fas on CD34+ cells driving apoptosis, and immune selection can produce HLA-loss and PNH clones. Genetically determined immune-response features (HLA, cytokine and T-cell polarization gene polymorphisms) likely convert a normal response into sustained autoimmunity, explaining why aplasia is rare despite common exposures. Idiosyncratic drug-induced aplasia is attributed to abnormal generation of or failure to detoxify reactive electrophilic drug intermediates that bind cellular macromolecules. Constitutional syndromes are intrinsic stem cell defects: Fanconi anemia involves a DNA interstrand cross-link repair pathway (most often FANCA; the gene products monoubiquitinate FANCD2), telomere biology disorders involve telomerase complex (DKC1, TERC, TERT) or shelterin (TINF2) defects that limit replicative capacity, and GATA2/RUNX1 mutations disrupt hematopoietic transcriptional regulation; Diamond-Blackfan and Shwachman-Diamond syndromes are ribosomopathies. MDS is a clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorder of aging marrow characterized by disordered proliferation, impaired differentiation and ineffective hematopoiesis producing cytopenias plus risk of leukemic progression; both chromosomal instability (non-random losses of 5, 7, 20, trisomy 8) and accumulating somatic mutations in ~100 recurrently mutated myeloid genes drive disease, with clonal succession of founder clones acquiring further mutations during evolution to AML.
additionalDifferentials: Hypoplastic/hypocellular MDS (most important and difficult distinction from aplastic anemia)
Constitutional vs acquired aplastic anemia (Fanconi anemia, telomere biology disorders, GATA2 and RUNX1 predisposition)
Acute leukemia / aleukemic leukemia and bone marrow lymphoma
Myelofibrosis and myelophthisis (marrow infiltration by tumor)
Vitamin B12, folate or copper deficiency causing cytopenias with dysplastic marrow
VEXAS syndrome (somatic UBA1 mutation) in MDS with inflammatory features
Systemic lupus erythematosus with marrow hypoplasia
Large granular lymphocytosis or thymoma associated cytopenias
infectionMimics: Persistent parvovirus B19 (pure red cell aplasia)
Seronegative (non-A, non-B, non-C) hepatitis preceding aplastic anemia
nonInfectiousMimics: Megaloblastic anemia from B12 or folate deficiency
Copper deficiency (and zinc or alcohol toxicity) causing dysplastic marrow with vacuolated precursors
additionalInvestigations: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy (biopsy >1 cm preferred) for cellularity and morphology; hypocellular marrow with <25% hematopoietic cells supports aplastic anemia
Peripheral smear and reticulocyte count (look for absent reticulocytes, large red cells, immature myeloid forms or nucleated red cells suggesting MDS/myelophthisis)
Flow cytometry for a PNH clone
Chromosome breakage testing with diepoxybutane or mitomycin C for Fanconi anemia (children and younger adults)
Peripheral blood leukocyte telomere length measurement for telomere biology disorders
Bone marrow cytogenetics and FISH (abnormal in MDS, expected normal in typical aplastic anemia)
Next-generation sequencing germline panels (50+ genes) for constitutional syndromes and myeloid neoplasm somatic panels (~100 genes) for MDS/AML, including spliceosome and cohesin genes
Serologies for EBV, HIV and viral hepatitis
Vitamin B12, folate and serum copper levels
Spinal MRI may demonstrate fatty marrow replacement in aplastic anemia
Parvovirus B19 DNA detection in suspected PRCA
Chest imaging to seek thymoma in PRCA and to exclude miliary tuberculosis
redFlags: Profound neutropenia (absolute neutrophil count <500/uL) with fever mandates urgent empirical broad-spectrum parenteral antibiotics without awaiting cultures
Persistent or recrudescent fever despite antibacterials implies invasive fungal disease (Candida, Aspergillus)
Severe thrombocytopenia with central nervous system or retinal bleeding can be catastrophic (intracranial or retinal hemorrhage)
Platelet count below 5000/uL sharply increases risk of gut bleeding
Systemic symptoms, weight loss, lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly point away from simple aplastic anemia toward malignancy or systemic disease
Emergence of new cytogenetic abnormalities, rising blasts, marrow fibrosis or abrupt worsening of pancytopenia signals clonal evolution to MDS/leukemia
Family history of AML/MDS or unexplained cytopenias should trigger evaluation for an inherited predisposition syndrome
harrison.prognosis: Untreated severe aplastic anemia deteriorates rapidly and is fatal; spontaneous recovery is rare. The dominant prognostic factor is the blood count: severe disease has historically required two of three of an absolute neutrophil count <500/uL, platelets <20,000/uL and corrected reticulocyte count <1% (or absolute reticulocytes <60,000/uL), while in the immunosuppression era higher absolute reticulocytes (>25,000/uL) and lymphocytes (>1000/uL) better predict response and survival. A PNH clone, very short telomeres and somatic myeloid mutations (e.g., ASXL1) further influence outcome and risk of clonal evolution. Clonal evolution to MDS or leukemia occurs in roughly 10-15% of immunosuppression-treated patients over a decade. In MDS, median survival ranges from years (5q- or sideroblastic anemia) to only months (high blast count disease); the IPSS-R and emerging molecularly informed IPSS-M stratify risk. Even lower-risk MDS carries meaningful morbidity and mortality; most patients die of complications of pancytopenia rather than leukemic transformation, and about a third die of unrelated comorbidities. Therapy-related MDS has an extremely poor prognosis with rapid progression to refractory AML. Pure red cell aplasia is generally compatible with long-term survival with supportive care, and persistent parvovirus B19 PRCA almost always responds to immunoglobulin.
pitfalls: Clinical drug/chemical and viral associations with aplastic anemia are not proof of causation; the implicated agent may merely have been used to treat the earliest symptoms (antibiotics for fever, NSAIDs causing petechiae in an already thrombocytopenic patient).

Marrow cellularity correlates imperfectly with disease severity: 'empty' biopsies can occur in moderate disease and focal 'hot spots' of hematopoiesis can be seen in severe aplasia, so a single small or dilute sample can mislead (a dry tap suggests fibrosis or myelophthisis rather than aplasia).

Distinguishing acquired from constitutional aplastic anemia is essential; constitutional marrow is usually morphologically indistinguishable and physical anomalies may be subtle or absent (adults with telomere disorders can present without anomalies, only premature graying).
Hypocellular MDS can be mistaken for aplastic anemia; the boundary with low-risk MDS is blurred (del 13q/20q may respond to immunosuppression, and DNMT3A/ASXL1 mutations occur in both).

Dysplastic marrow changes are not specific to MDS, occurring with vitamin deficiencies, copper deficiency, drug effects, alcohol and acute viral infection; interobserver agreement on dysplasia morphology is imperfect.
Germline genomic panel results may take weeks to return, a problem in the severely pancytopenic patient who needs prompt management.
In transplant-eligible aplastic anemia patients, transfusing blood from family members risks alloimmunization and should be avoided; HLA typing should be ordered as soon as the diagnosis is made.
Glucocorticoids are not effective primary therapy for aplastic anemia and increase fungal infection risk.
harrison.severityClassification: Severe aplastic anemia has historically been defined by the presence of at least two of three criteria: absolute neutrophil count <500/uL, platelet count <20,000/uL, and corrected reticulocyte count <1% (or absolute reticulocyte count <60,000/uL). In the immunosuppressive-therapy era, absolute reticulocyte count >25,000/uL and absolute lymphocyte count >1000/uL are better predictors of response and long-term outcome. For MDS, prognostic severity is assessed by the Revised International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS-R), which integrates marrow blast percentage (categories at <=2%, >2-<5%, 5-10%, >10-30%), refined cytogenetic risk groups, depth of cytopenias (hemoglobin, platelets, neutrophils), and additional features (age, performance status, ferritin, LDH, beta-2-microglobulin) into five risk categories; the molecularly enhanced IPSS-M is emerging as the current standard.
